job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior data engineer at an insurance company in Edinburgh. I studied computer science, and my final project was a tool that spotted duplicate claims. Most days I build data pipelines, fix the ones that broke overnight, and use an AI assistant for about half my code. I share a flat with a friend from uni, Hana, and we split everything down the middle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle side of it, finding why a number is wrong. What I don't like is the loan and the money. I'm on an entry salary, I have about a week of cushion, and my parents live abroad and can't help. I check my balance more often than I check my email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I use the tools every day and they're useful, but they make mistakes, so a person still has to check. I'd tell friends to enjoy the time-saving and not expect miracles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about the work and not okay about money. Insurance is steady, but my team is small, and juniors are cheaper to cut than seniors. I'd also hate to be here for years paying the loan with no raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the dull parts and spend the saved time on things the team notices, like cleaning up the claims data that nobody wants to touch. I'd put 70 a month into savings and ask for a review of my pay at the one-year mark. I'd also keep learning one new tool each quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little tight. Steady at work, tight with money, and I can live with that for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pay review look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring a list of things I fixed or built, with dates and numbers. My manager, Callum, likes evidence, and I've learned that asking without it just gets a nice smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you mean by cheaper to cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If budgets tighten, firms cut the people whose absence is felt least. I'm pretty sure that's juniors, even good ones, so I try to be noticed by making a visible difference.

say: The tools are **useful but make mistakes**, so a person still has to check.
I'd tell friends not to expect miracles.
think: I'm okay about the work but not about **money**, and juniors are cheaper to cut.
I'd hate paying the loan for years with **no raise**.
do: Use AI for dull work and clean up **claims data** nobody wants.
Ask for a **pay review** at one year, with a list of results.
feel: **A little tight**, steady at work and tight with money.
S0.quote: I'd tell friends to enjoy the time-saving and not expect miracles.
fieldNote: Her unease is a **junior's position** and a thin cushion.
She prepares evidence before asking for anything.
Uses AI naturally, without hype, and treats it as an everyday work tool.

steps.text: Clean up the claims data nobody wants to touch
Learn one new data tool every quarter
Move 70 a month into savings and ask for a pay review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the world I'm already in. I'd tell friends that if you can use AI well, you're worth more, and if you can't, you should start now. I'd say it quietly, though, because not everyone wants to hear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of a knife edge. Coding and checking are exactly the tasks the card says go first, and I'm a junior. On the other hand, I'm the sort of person who adapts quickly, so I'd bet on myself but I wouldn't bet the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward the part of the work that's about understanding the business and the customer, not typing code. I'd ask Callum to put me on the project with the claims team, so I can learn the insurance side. I'd also build a small public portfolio of work and keep a month of rent in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy together. Like starting a new school halfway through the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bet on yourself but not the rent. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd try things, but I'd keep a cushion so a failed experiment doesn't mean missed rent. I'd aim for one month of rent in cash by the end of the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the people who can't adapt quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry about them. Hana's brother is a developer who doesn't like new tools, and he's already being passed over, so I'd want some real help for people like him.

say: That's the **world I'm already in**, and people should learn AI tools now.
I'd say it quietly because not everyone wants to hear it.
think: Coding and checking go first, and I'm a **junior**, so it's a knife edge.
I'd bet on myself but **not the rent**.
do: Ask Callum to put me on the **claims team** project to learn the insurance side.
Build a small public **portfolio** of work.
Hold **one month** of rent in cash by year end.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**, like starting a new school halfway through the year.
S1.quote: I'd try things, but I'd keep a cushion so a failed experiment doesn't mean missed rent.
fieldNote: She is **adaptive** but honest about being exposed as a junior coder.
Wants to move toward business understanding.
Cares about colleagues who adapt slowly, and wants real help for them.

steps.text: Join the claims team project to learn the insurance side
Use AI tools daily and publish a small portfolio
Hold one month of rent in cash by year end
Take an evening course in insurance and risk basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd say it directly. Governments and companies need to be honest about what they know, and they need to be planning right now. I'd also tell friends to use the tools, since the choice isn't between using them and not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my kind of job goes quite quickly. A junior data engineer is exactly the type of person a thinking AI replaces, and the robots at 2031 don't help me. I'm adaptable, but there'd be a lot of adaptable people chasing very few jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up as much cash as I could in the first six months and cut my rent by moving to a cheaper room. I'd look for jobs that need a person in the room, like working with customers on claims, or care and health systems. And I'd try to use the AI tools to start something small of my own, since I'd have the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also weirdly awake. My brain goes fast, and I make lists at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the list at three in the morning say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay the rent, keep two months in cash, call Callum about what's coming, check my loan terms, and ask my parents if they'd help if the worst happened. It would also say don't tell anyone how scared you are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not tell anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to be the person who panics first. At work, calm gets you trust, and I'd need that trust more than ever.

say: It's **too fast**, and governments and companies must plan now.
Using the tools is no longer optional, and I'd tell friends so.
think: A junior data engineer is exactly what a **thinking AI** replaces.
Many adaptable people would be chasing **very few jobs**.
do: Build cash for six months and move to a **cheaper room**.
Look for jobs that need a person with **customers** or in health systems.
Try a **small business** of my own with AI tools.
feel: **Scared but awake**, making lists at three in the morning.
S2.quote: At work, calm gets you trust, and I'd need that trust more than ever.
fieldNote: She is anxious but **acts quickly**, producing lists and plans.
Hides her fear at work to keep trust, and shows it only in private lists.

steps.text: Keep two months of rent in cash within six months
Move to a cheaper room in a shared flat
Apply for customer-facing claims and health systems roles
Start a small data tool business using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to adapt, and I'd say so confidently. I'd tell friends to learn a mix of technical and people skills, because the second kind lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like I have a head start, since I'm already using the tools every day. But being a junior now means being a senior in 2031, and I'd want to be a senior who manages AI systems, not one who competes with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the insurer for two years and become the person who knows the claims data best. Then I'd move into a role that checks and directs AI, maybe at a regulator or a bigger firm. I'd pay the loan down by 150 a month and keep three months of rent in an account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Five years feels like a game I can play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the regulator?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to check AI models used in insurance, and the rules will get tougher. If I know the data and the tools, I'd be useful on either side of the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything is moving faster than the card says, or the regulator also uses AI to do the checking. I can't rule it out, so I'd keep a second option, like the small business.

say: Five years is **enough to adapt**, and people skills last longer than technical ones.
I'd tell friends to learn both.
think: I'd have a **head start**, as I use the tools daily.
I want to be a senior who **directs AI**, not competes with it.
do: Become the person who knows the **claims data** best.
Move to a role that **checks AI** at a regulator or a bigger firm.
Pay **150 a month** toward the loan and keep three months of rent.
feel: **Pretty good**, since five years feels like a game I can play.
S3.quote: Being a junior now means being a senior in 2031, and I'd want to be a senior who manages AI systems, not one who competes with them.
fieldNote: She thinks about **seniority in 2031**, which shows long-range planning.
Keeps a second option in case the plan fails.
Confidence comes from daily AI use.

steps.text: Become the team's expert on the claims data
Apply to a regulator or larger firm that checks AI models
Pay 150 a month toward the loan
Keep a small data-tools side business as a second option

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long, and I'd say it's time to think about what we want from the technology, not just what it does. I'd say people should plan, but without being scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as an opportunity. I'd be 32 and I'd have time to become senior, get out of debt, and maybe start my own firm. The one thing I'd worry about is not noticing the moment things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, clear the loan within five years and save a deposit for a flat. I'd learn one new AI skill every year, like model checking, or language processing, so I'd keep pace. I'd also stay in touch with the people from uni, since they'd be my network when the world shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit curious. I'd like to see how it turns out, and I'd like to have a hand in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to notice the moment things change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading the people who build this stuff, and watching hiring in my own field. If the graduate postings drop by half, that's a signal, whatever the date on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay in touch with uni friends. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because jobs come through people. When Hana found her post, it was via a friend of her sister's, and I'd like my friends to be the ones who hear first, and for me to hear first from them.

say: Ten years is long, so think about **what we want** from the technology.
People should plan but not be scared.
think: I'd see it as an **opportunity** to become senior and get out of debt.
I'd worry most about **not noticing** the moment things change.
do: Clear the loan in **five years** and save a flat deposit.
Learn one new **AI skill** every year.
Stay in touch with **uni friends** as a network.
feel: **Calm and curious**, wanting a hand in how it turns out.
S4.quote: If the graduate postings drop by half, that's a signal, whatever the date on the card.
fieldNote: Only **calm** scenario; adaptability and time line up for her.
Watches hiring data as her own warning signal.
Values personal networks for finding jobs, which fits her sociable, adaptive style.

steps.text: Clear the student loan within five years
Learn one new AI skill every year, such as model checking
Save a deposit for a flat once the loan is gone
Watch graduate hiring numbers in my field each quarter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time to clear a loan or build savings, and the jobs I'd go for would all be gone at once. What would help is a loan that pauses if you lose work, and a clear public plan for people starting out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that adaptable doesn't mean unafraid. I use these tools every day, and I still lie awake wondering what happens to my loan.

headlineQuote: Adaptable doesn't mean unafraid. I use these tools every day, and I still lie awake wondering what happens to my loan.
portrait: Elena, 22, is a top computer science graduate working as a junior data engineer at an **Edinburgh insurer**.
She has heavy debt, about a week of savings, and parents abroad who can't help.
She is centrist and adaptive, using AI tools every day and always asking what evidence supports a move.
Junior coding is exposed, so she aims to become the one who **directs and checks** AI.
She is uneasy in slower worlds, anxious when time is short, and calm only with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, since no time or cushion exists to clear the loan.
whatWouldHelp: A **loan pause** if work ends, and a clear public plan for people just starting out.
